h012: Some law of nature produced this. Can you find it?
h015: What happens as the population gets larger?
h019: Choose a prediction. Watch its curve meet the measurements.
h020: A curve tells us what happened. An equation tries to tell us why. WISP builds possible equations a piece at a time, then asks whether they reproduce the behaviour we measured.
h029: Imagine a population. Its size is called
h031: . A differential equation tells us how quickly that size changes at this moment. To draw a curve, take a small step in time, update the size using the rule, and repeat.
h032: The symbol on the left means “change in population per unit of time.” On the right,
h036: is the capacity. Near capacity, growth slows. Move either slider to see a rule become a curve.
h039: Illustration. The starting population stays fixed; each point follows from the previous point and the rule.
h041: Prey feed predators; predators eat prey. We need a rule for each population. The time plot shows when each rises and falls. The phase plane plots prey against predators: time is now the journey around the loop.
h043: Illustration of the cookbook’s predator–prey system. The marked point is the same moment in both views. Dashed line: predators; solid line: prey.
h046: Now reverse the question. We have measurements, but we do not know the rule. Start with a catalogue of building blocks, called
h048: . A coefficient tells us how strongly each term acts. Switching on a term chooses a piece of the equation.
h051: are present. Parameters are their coefficients. A curve can look right even when its structure is wrong.
h053: describes interaction between variables; it appears when we have more than one variable.
h055: Illustration: adjust terms and coefficients; no model is fitted.
h056: Trying every combination gets expensive quickly. Choose how many variables a system has. Each equation can use any subset of its catalogue; the total counts below include all equations and the empty subset.
h058: A small disturbance, a big problem
h060: A measurement is never perfect. Here each value is multiplied by a small random disturbance. The same disturbances are reused as you move the noise slider, so you see only the effect of their size.
h061: A slope estimate subtracts neighbouring measurements and divides by their time gap. When the gap is small, a tiny measurement error becomes a large slope error. Compare the nearly smooth measurements with the jagged derivative estimate.
h063: Real Q5 observations at the recorded noise level; rescaled noise is an illustration. Solid truth curve; dotted noisy estimate. This slider also updates the weak-form and growth figures below.
h064: Replace a slope with a total
h066: Instead of asking how fast the population changed at a single moment, ask how much it changed across a window. The left side is the last measurement minus the first. The right side adds up the rule over the same window. “Integral” is the mathematical name for that total.
h067: Each shaded area below is a candidate term’s integral. Multiply the areas by coefficients and add them: the result should match the measured change. Integration accumulates nearby values instead of dividing their differences by a small time gap. It helps with noise; it does not make noise disappear.
h070: Drag across the main curve to move the window, or use the keyboard controls above.
h071: Dashed: clean integrals. Solid: integrals of noisy measurements. The trapezoidal rule joins adjacent measurements with straight lines and adds their areas.
h073: Repeat this for overlapping windows of several lengths. Every row below is one window; every column is one candidate term. We now seek coefficients that make the weighted columns match the change column. This is linear regression: the terms may be curved, but their coefficients enter as a weighted sum.
h074: A preview of the stacked system. Select a row to inspect its window. Remaining rows use the same construction. The target column comes from measurements, never the true equation.
h075: A short list, one decision at a time
h077: WISP starts with no terms. FROLS tries each unused term, refits all current coefficients, and chooses the largest reduction in remaining squared error. A large bar means useful
h079: information given what is already selected, rather than a good match in isolation.
h080: FoBa then asks whether an older term has become redundant. It removes the cheapest term when its removal costs less than the permitted fraction of the latest forward gain. That lets an early guess leave when a better explanation arrives.
h084: Forward gains are measured before the addition. The equation and residual show the joint refit after backward removals. Squared error refers to the stacked weak system, not trajectory quality.
h086: The live example follows the frozen interim growth policy. Its cap and near-zero residual stop are displayed beside the path. This is an interim policy, not a claim that model size has been solved.
h089: Another term can lower the training error even when it only follows noise. A path needs an end. In Q5 the interim cap is six terms per equation: twice the largest true equation size. This uses knowledge of the answer and is a declared limitation.
h090: The Q7 significance rule asks a different question: does any remaining term help more than noise plausibly could? Noise is estimated from nearby measurements, then carried into the weak form. Growth stops when every remaining gain is below the significance threshold relative to its expected noise gain. The numerical-zero and cycle checks still apply.
h092: The noise floor is an expected residual, not a rule to stop at that height. Q7 tests the gain from the next term. This is a live rule demonstration on Q5 observations, not a Q7 result rate.
h093: From a short list to one model
h095: Every state on the path is a candidate. Each gets one trajectory fit, started from its weak coefficients. The fit adjusts the coefficients so the simulated curve follows the observed measurements. The true equation and the second starting point do not take part in this choice.
h096: BIC balances fit and size. Better fit lowers the score; every coefficient adds a penalty. The smallest score wins. Here the penalty per coefficient is the logarithm of the number of observed scalar values. It guards against buying a tiny improvement with a more complicated equation.
h098: Take the second trajectory out of the fridge
h099: The real test: a second starting point
h100: Keep a second measurement series in the fridge while the model learns. Only now take it out. Start the chosen equation at that other clean starting point, with the same coefficients. Reconstruction checks the clean training trajectory. Generalization checks the second trajectory, which was never used for training or choosing.
h102: Measurements reveal only the states they visit. A missing true term cannot be repaired by fitting the candidates afterwards. Noise can hide the distinction between different equations. Oscillations can be very sensitive to the starting state. Initial-state estimation, coefficient bounds and the stopping rule still depend on their stated gates. Comparisons with the original WSINDy implementation need their documented checks; ablations must test what each component contributes. These interim examples do not settle those questions.
h106: Recovering the exact terms and drawing the right curve are different achievements. Both stay visible below. Reconstruction starts from the clean training initial condition; generalization starts from the other initial condition. The curve metric asks how often the model explains enough variation to cross the displayed threshold.
h107: Only exact systems enter these structure rates. Strata stay separate. Counts are cells; repeated initial conditions and noise draws do not create independent systems. No uncertainty interval or significance claim is inferred from the cell count.
h112: Rates are rounded for display; their exported values and counts retain the aggregation’s precision.
h114: Choose a stratum above, then a system and a cell. The equations come from the stored trajectory-BIC choice. Curves appear only after their re-simulation passes the recorded-score check.
h120: A rule for the rate of change at the current state.
h122: The curve produced by following a rule from a starting state.
h124: A building block of a rule / the number multiplying that block.
h126: The equation integrated across windows, replacing local derivatives with accumulated change.
h128: The difference between a measured target and the model’s prediction for it.
h130: The set of terms present in the equation. Raw uses every stored term; pruned removes small coefficients using the frozen evaluation rule.
h132: A score comparing prediction error with variation around the data’s mean. A perfect prediction reaches unity; a score below zero is worse than predicting the mean.
h134: A separate group of systems / a particular initial condition, noise and sampling draw / an underlying equation.
h136: An information criterion trading fit against model size. A smaller score wins.
h138: WISP combines established pieces. The weak form makes the search less sensitive to numerical derivatives; incremental growth keeps a short candidate list; backward removal lets early guesses leave; simulation and refitting test behaviour over time.

x7_headline: Nature describes itself in rates of change
x7_deck: How fast does a bacterial culture grow? How fast does a coffee cool? How fast does a flu spread? A differential equation does not say where something is, but how fast it is changing right now. That one rule produces the whole course: it explains why something happens, predicts what comes next, and can be tested against new measurements.
x7_caption: Bacteria in a dish: two colonies grow steadily outward at their rim. The bigger they get, the longer their rim and the more cells are added at once. When space runs short, growth slows until the dish is full. Behind this S-shaped course sits a simple rule. Illustration, not measured data.
x7_station1: Kepler reads fixed patterns from Tycho Brahe's planetary observations; Newton turns them into a rule for how motion changes — Kepler's laws follow from it.
x7_station2: Verhulst derives the rule for slowing growth from census data — the same one as in the dish above.
x7_station3: Lotka and Volterra explain with two coupled equations why predators and prey rise and fall in turn in the Adriatic fish-market records.
x7_station4: Hodgkin and Huxley build the equations of the nerve impulse from measurements on a squid's nerve fibre (Nobel Prize 1963).
x7_station5: Data come in floods, time for handwork does not. Methods such as SINDy (2016) search for the equation automatically — WISP is one of them.

x9_deck: WISP starts with an empty equation. First it tries each of the six blocks on its own: how well does it alone explain how u changes?
x9_caption: How much of the explainable changes each block alone explains. The rest is measurement noise — no block explains that.
x9_total: How much of the total measured changes each block alone explains.
x9_result: {winner} explains the most{explain_constant}. WISP takes it as the first block of the equation.
x9_constant: — a constant growth rate. Not bad as a rough first guess
x9_recorded: First step of the recorded WISP run on exactly these measurements.

x10_title_1: What we want to describe: the change
x10_text_0: Measurements of u were taken at {n} times between t = {t0} and t = {t1} — with {noise} noise. WISP has nothing else.
x10_text_1: A differential equation says how u changes. So we extract exactly that from the measurements: how much u changes over a time interval. Between two adjacent points, noise almost drowns out the signal — longer intervals reveal the pattern.
x10_text_2: An empty equation says: u never changes. Every measured change is then an error. We square each discrepancy and add them all up — this is the error without a block. We set it to 100%.
x10_text_3: Take block 1: du/dt = c. The equation predicts a change of c × length for each interval. Which c is best? The one that makes the error smallest.
x10_text_4: WISP tries each block on its own. The number in the equation changes until the error is smallest. Then the block receives its bar. After each attempt the bars sort by explained share, best at the top.
x10_text_5: Part of every measured change is measurement noise. No block can explain it — whichever. As just seen, WISP estimates this part from the data: {floor} of the error. So only {explainable} is explainable.
x10_text_6: The {winner} explains the most — {meaning}. That is a useful first approximation. WISP takes it as its first block:
x10_caption: Shown: intervals that do not overlap. WISP computes with all intervals of all lengths. All errors, percentages and block coefficients here use that full computation.
x10_weak: In technical terms: weak form; numerical differences over time windows
x10_noise: In technical terms: error reduction ratio; noise estimation
x10_frols: In technical terms: first step of FROLS (Forward Regression Orthogonal Least Squares)
x10_direct: There is no need to search for this number: since the prediction is simply c times something, the best c can be calculated directly.
x10_r2: This number is an R² — on the changes over intervals, and calculated only on the explainable part: 100% would mean explaining everything that can be explained.
x10_next: What happens next — which block is added — comes in the next chapter.
x10_clipped: {n} points lie outside and are shown at the edge
x10_fallback: Noise floor unavailable; shares use the total error.
x11_noise_result: Estimated this way: noise of on average {est} of u. The noise actually added was {true} — the estimate is close. Every change u(end) − u(start) picks up the noise of both end points. Added up over all windows this gives {floor} of the error without a block: the part no block can explain.
x12_title_2: What a differential equation describes: the slope
x12_title_8: How do we know how much noise there is?
x12_text_0: u was measured at {n} times between t = {t0} and t = {t1}. That is all WISP has.
x12_text_1: Each point is a little way off the true curve: that is measurement noise, here {noise}. WISP does not know the true curve — we show it only to make the noise visible.
x12_text_2: A differential equation says how steep the curve is at each point — how fast u is changing right now. That is exactly what WISP wants to find out from the measurements.
x12_text_3: Two neighbouring points give an estimate of the slope: the change in u divided by the time between them. Because both points carry noise and are close together, the result is almost all noise. The green line shows the true slope: how fast u is changing right now. WISP tries to recover this change per unit of time; the secants estimate it. WISP does not know this reference line.
x12_text_4: With short sections the estimated slopes scatter widely; with longer ones they lie closer to the true slope. For each length ({lengths} sampling gaps) we draw six sections side by side; with each length the view zooms out and shows more measurements. The bars show the typical deviation from the true slope.
x12_text_8: Over a short stretch, the real curve is smooth. WISP fits a smooth curve (a cubic polynomial) through each set of 9 neighbouring measurements. The distance of the centre point from it is almost all noise. WISP does this for every point.
x12_actual: Recalculating with the true curve would give {actual}. (Calculation for this presentation.)
x12_noise_result: Estimated noise: {est}; actually added: {true}. Noise at both endpoints adds up over all windows to {floor} of the error without a block. No block can explain this part.
x12c_chapter: Chapter 1 · One block on its own
x12c_noise_title: Why WISP needs to know the noise
x12c_noise_text: Even the best block leaves a large error. Part of it is measurement noise — no equation can explain that. To avoid trying to explain noise, WISP needs to know how large that part is.
x12c_question: How much of this is just noise?
x12c_sum_1: Noise at the start + end of each window,
x12c_floor: {floor} of the error without a block
x13_text_0: Chapter one ended with one block: du/dt = {c}, a constant slope. It explains {before} of what can be explained at all — a little over half. The points are again the slopes from long sections; the line is the prediction.
x13_text_1: The vertical strokes show what the prediction misses. If this were only noise, the points would lie randomly above and below the line, mostly within the band — that is how far noise typically spreads. Instead they follow a pattern: in the first half almost all lie above the line, in the second half almost all below. A pattern is not chance, so more can be explained.
x13_text_2: Let us try u as a second block. Important: WISP does not keep the first number. Both numbers are determined anew together, so that the total error becomes as small as possible — the constant moves away from {c}. The line may now slope.
x13_text_3: WISP tries every remaining block as a partner for the constant, refitting both numbers each time. After each attempt the bars sort by explained share, best at the top. WISP selects the highest value: {term}.
x13_text_4: With {term} as the second block, the explained share rises from {before} to {after}. So the error sinks. The noise part stays as it is — no block can make it smaller.
x13_text_5: This is the equation after the second step. The number in front of {term} looks tiny, but {term} grows to about {maximum} in these data — tiny times large gives a noticeable contribution to the slope.
x13_closing: Whether this is already the right equation — and what WISP does next — is the next chapter.
x13_jargon: In technical terms: second step of FROLS (Forward Regression Orthogonal Least Squares); all numbers are re-estimated jointly by least squares.

x17_title_1: The probe: leave each block out once
x17_text_0: Our model explains {share} of the explainable part. No block has left yet. But a new block can make an old one redundant. Does each still pull its weight?
x17_text_1: Leave each block out once and refit the rest. How much does the residual increase? Each bar shows the explained share we would lose.
x17_text_2: Both bars lie above the threshold, so both stay. Each add/remove pair still reduces the residual by at least half the gain. The procedure cannot run in circles and is guaranteed to end. The factor {fraction} is Zhang’s published default; we did not tune it.
x17_text_3: Add {linear}. Leaving out the constant now costs less than half the new gain, so it goes. Refit the rest and probe again. Repeat until nothing leaves.
x17_text_4: With {quadratic}, {cubic} becomes redundant. Its loss is almost invisible, so it is labelled. It goes. Probe every remaining block again: both stay.
x17_text_5: For the first time we show the true equation of the teaching system. Its blocks match the last FoBa model. Compare the weak-fit coefficients beside it. EvoGrow had no such backward step: a wrong block could never leave again.
x17_text_6: Each box is a candidate. Adding {next} would yield another {gain} on the same scale. Before WISP adds anything, the test in the next chapter decides whether the path continues.
x17_more: The rule comes from Tong Zhang’s FoBa algorithm. A forward step reduces the residual by a gain. A backward step may increase it again, but by less than half that gain. Each such pair retains at least half as improvement. The residual falls, the procedure cannot run in circles and is guaranteed to end. After each removal, probe again until no block falls below the threshold. Zhang also proves recovery of the true structure under specific conditions; this is no general promise for noisy data.
x17_caption: Weak fit on the same windows as before; every removal cost includes refitting the rest.
x17_forward: Without clean-up – not what WISP does
x18_text_0: Gains shrink. But even pure noise would let every extra block explain something. Is the gain larger than that? The noise estimate from the first chapter remains our reference.
x18_text_1: The model is now {support}. If the data were only noise of the measured size, adding a block would still lower the residual by about the pale bar. Its actual gain is beside it, on the same scale.
x18_text_2: Divide gain by noise expectation. The threshold {threshold} is the {percent}th percentile of χ² with {df} degree of freedom: pure Gaussian noise exceeds it per tested block in only {one} out of {hundred} cases. No bar reaches it; even {best} is only at {ratio}. The path ends at {support}. The axis is logarithmic.
x18_title_3: Every round, in the right order
x18_text_3: Test first: does any open block help clearly more than noise? Only then add the block with the largest gain. Next probe every block, remove the cheapest below half the new gain and probe again. When the test fails, there is no addition or clean-up.
x18_text_4: These candidates remain. Which is the right one? The weak space cannot decide on its own. In the next chapter we simulate each candidate.
x18_caption: Live from the observations: test → add → clean up.
x19_title_0: From weak space back to the curve
x19_text_0: The path has ended. Weak coefficients are only an approximation: noise also enters the integrals. Small errors in the right-hand side accumulate over time. What matters now is whether the model reproduces the whole curve.
x19_text_1: BFGS starts at the weak coefficients and fits each candidate to the measured curve with exactly one attempt; the starting point is estimated too, because the first measurement is noisy as well. The weak start already lies in the right valley. MSE is the mean squared deviation over all observations; the stored reconstruction R² scores the curve.
x19_text_2: Only after the path ends is each candidate fitted once, shown here in path order with identical axes. Almost all of WISP’s compute goes into this step, which makes a short candidate list valuable.
x19_text_3: BIC rewards fit and charges a price per block. N is observations times dimension; k is the number of terms. An additional block pays only if it reduces MSE by more than {share}. Smaller wins. No tuning knob.
x19_text_4: The minimum is computed from the candidates’ stored BIC values. The fitted equation, the true equation and the weak start appear side by side in the comparison.
x19_text_5: Short sections turn observations into a short list. Test, add and clean up repeat until the test fails. Only then does each candidate receive one trajectory fit; finally, the smallest BIC chooses.
x19_settings: BFGS; exactly one attempt; coefficients in [−{bound}, {bound}]; simulation starts at: {initial}.
x19_fit_more: Why fit again? Noise biases the weak coefficients, and many well-fitted short windows do not guarantee a good whole trajectory. The trajectory fit corrects accumulated errors. Why not start there? The optimization problem has many valleys, and random starts often land in the wrong one. The weak form supplies a good start. A known weakness remains the noisy first observation that initializes the simulation.
x19_bic_more: BIC, due to Schwarz ({year}), reads fit as probability: for Gaussian errors, N × log(MSE) is minus twice the log-likelihood up to a constant. k × log(N) is the parameter price arising from averaging over plausible parameter values. Known weakness: errors along a simulated curve are correlated in time. BIC assumes independent errors, overestimates the information and tends toward larger models under noise.

x20_chapter6: Chapter 6 · And if there are several equations?
x20_remains_body: On the same scale as adding a block: noise floor, explained by the final weak model, and the still explainable remainder.
x20_system_body: So far every measurement had one quantity. Now hares and foxes live on a meadow, and each species has its own equation: hares multiply and are eaten, foxes die without food and multiply by eating. WISP looks for both equations at once, each with its own box of building blocks.
x20_system: {equation} · Initial state: {start} · Noise: {sigma} · {blocks} blocks per equation
x20_rounds_body: Test each equation, add one block, then clean up. In the test, bar and number show the gain divided by the noise gain (logarithmic axis). For the addition, the gain is divided by the size of that equation's left-hand side, so both equations compete fairly.
x20_stop_body: In each equation every remaining gain is below the test threshold.
x20_candidates_body: Each path state receives one trajectory fit. BIC combines error and model size; the smallest value wins.
x20_winner: Selected: {candidate} · Structure raw / pruned: {raw} / {pruned} · Reconstruction R² {rec} · Generalization R² {gen}
x20_coefficients: True parameters: {truth} · Fitted parameters (equation order, signed): {fit}
x20_orbit_title: The structure is right. What about the curve?
x20_orbit_body: On the left the model starts at the estimated initial state, as it was fitted; on the right at the true start. The stored reconstruction score belongs to the right panel. Both curves coincide: the estimated start lies practically on the true one.
x20_errors: Training MSE: noisy start {noisy_initial_training_mse} · true start {true_initial_training_mse}
x20_lesson_title: Measure structure and curve agreement separately
x20_lesson_body: Structure and curve are both right. Estimating the initial state helps: the first measurement is noisy too, and in oscillating systems a wrong start shifts the whole curve.
x20_gate_pending: G2 pending: variant C, estimate the initial state jointly.
x20_failure_title: The same equation, a different start
x20_failure_body: The upper part of the growth curve makes some building blocks harder to distinguish.
x20_start: Start here {here}, teaching example {other}; same noise {sigma}.
x20_failure_rounds_title: The truth never reaches the list
x20_failure_rounds_body: Nothing is removed. The constant stays. The quadratic truth block brings less than the noise threshold: stop.
x20_rhs_body: Different right-hand sides agree over the observed range. Below it, they diverge.
x20_failure_lesson_title: A good curve does not guarantee the right structure
x20_failure_lesson_body: In this example, WISP does not recover the true structure from the observations, although the selected model matches the trajectory well. Structure and curve agreement are therefore reported together.
x20_measured_body: Reconstruction: the same model from the true training initial state against the clean training trajectory. Generalization: unchanged parameters, starting at the other initial state, compared with its clean trajectory.
x20_trajectory_title: The teaching example at the other initial state
x20_trajectory_body: No new fit: start the selected model at the other initial state.
x20_comparison_title: Three examples, two kinds of success
x20_comparison_body: Structure and trajectory scores sometimes disagree. These scores use variance weighting.
x20_metric: Literature metric: share of cases with R² > {threshold}.
x20_close_body: The next chapter shows how often structure recovery and generalization succeed. Use the results explorer to inspect individual conditions and systems.
